title: Encryption of customer data at rest in production stores and backups
status_rationale: SOC2-014 requires encryption to be defined and enforced; SEC-CRYPTO-001 requires managed keys; no store, provider or key service exists.
target_answer: Every production data store that holds customer data, including managed PostgreSQL storage, replicas, snapshots, backups, object storage for statements and documents, search indexes, AI embeddings, caches, queues and logs, is encrypted at rest with AES-256 under keys held in the cloud key management service (ANS-ENC-004). Encryption is not optional: an organization guardrail denies creating unencrypted storage (ECTL-CLD-004) and a daily check attests that every store in the data location inventory is encrypted with an approved key. Community PostgreSQL has no built-in transparent data encryption, so storage-level encryption is provided by the managed service; the most sensitive fields additionally receive application-level encryption (ANS-ENC-008) so that database administrators and backups do not expose them in plaintext.
current_practice: Not established. Hosting provider, regions and managed services for Unbound are not selected (no verified production infrastructure exists as of 2026-11-25).
intended_practice: Enable provider storage encryption with customer-managed provider keys from day one; add guardrail and daily attestation.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: all customer data at rest, including backups and logs, encrypted with AES-256 under keys in a managed key service, with encryption enforced by policy. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Storage-level encryption protects against media theft and some provider-side access, not against an attacker using the application's or database's legitimate access.
Data in memory and in use is not protected by encryption at rest.
open_questions: Which managed PostgreSQL and object storage services will be used, and do they support customer-managed keys for all data including backups and replicas?

title: Encryption in transit over public networks
target_answer: All external connections to Unbound (browser, partner API, webhooks, file delivery) use TLS 1.3, with TLS 1.2 permitted only with forward-secret AEAD cipher suites (ECDHE with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305); TLS 1.0 and 1.1, SSL, RC4, 3DES, CBC-mode and static RSA key exchange are disabled. HSTS is set with a long max-age and includeSubDomains. Certificates are issued by approved CAs (CAA-restricted), use RSA 2048+ or ECDSA P-256+, are renewed automatically and monitored for expiry. Outbound connections to providers (payment, custodian, identity, email, AI model endpoints) require TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation; disabling validation is prohibited in code and detected by analysis. A weekly external scan verifies the configuration (ECTL-NET-009).
intended_practice: Encode TLS policy in edge configuration and an outbound HTTP client wrapper; add external scan.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 minimum with strong cipher suites) for all external connections, HSTS, and automatic certificate management. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Some partners or older bank systems may require TLS 1.2 cipher suites outside the preferred set; exceptions must be scoped to that integration.
open_questions: Do any target payment, custodian or bank integrations require legacy TLS versions or mutual TLS with specific certificate authorities?

title: Encryption in transit inside the hosting environment
target_answer: Every internal hop that carries customer data is encrypted and authenticated: edge to application (re-encrypted TLS), application to PostgreSQL (TLS with full certificate and hostname verification, for example Npgsql SSL Mode VerifyFull with the provider's CA pinned in configuration), application to key service, object storage and other managed services (TLS via provider SDKs or private endpoints). Connection settings are produced by a typed configuration module so a non-verifying mode cannot be configured without a failing build check. Database server settings reject non-TLS connections.
intended_practice: Build the typed connection configuration in the persistence layer (ADR-003 in the persistence design).
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: all internal connections, including to the database, encrypted with TLS and full certificate verification. Not yet implemented.
open_questions: Does the selected managed PostgreSQL service allow enforcing TLS-only connections server-side?

title: Key management lifecycle and custody
status_rationale: SEC-CRYPTO-001 calls for managed keys; persistence design ADR-006 (key management) is unresolved; UNB-TEN-006 and UNB-TEN-008 require partner-scoped keys where contracted.
target_answer: Keys are held in the cloud provider's key management service backed by FIPS 140-3 validated hardware security modules; key-encryption keys never leave the HSM boundary. Unbound uses envelope encryption: per-tenant key-encryption keys in KMS wrap data-encryption keys generated per tenant and per data class. Key policies separate duties: the application identity can encrypt and decrypt with its tenant keys but cannot change policies or schedule deletion; key administrators cannot use keys to decrypt data; deletion requires two-person approval and a waiting period. Every key use and administrative action is logged to the security log account. Keys rotate automatically at least annually (data keys more often), and a compromise procedure re-wraps or re-encrypts affected data. The key inventory, owners and policies are maintained as code.
current_practice: Not established. ADR-006 (key management, PII vault, lawful erasure) in TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN.md is open.
intended_practice: Resolve ADR-006 with the hosting decision; codify key hierarchy and policies.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: keys in a cloud KMS backed by validated HSMs, per-tenant envelope encryption, separation of key administration from key use, logged key operations and automatic rotation. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: The cloud provider operates the HSMs; provider insiders and legal compulsion against the provider are outside Echelon's control.
KMS outage blocks decryption and therefore service; cached data keys trade availability against exposure time.
open_questions: Cloud KMS (multi-tenant HSM-backed) or dedicated single-tenant HSM? Which customers, if any, require dedicated HSMs?
Requirements disagree on default isolation profile (CNV-ARC-001 schema per sponsor versus RR-UNB-PLAT-008-r1 dedicated database), which changes how keys are scoped per tenant.

title: FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules
status_rationale: No module selection exists. .NET does not implement its own cryptographic primitives: on Linux it uses the platform OpenSSL library and on Windows the CNG library, so FIPS validation depends on the OS module and its configuration, not on .NET.
target_answer: Data at rest is encrypted by cloud services whose key management uses FIPS 140-3 (or still-valid FIPS 140-2) validated HSMs, with certificate numbers recorded. In the application, cryptography goes through .NET APIs backed by the platform library; the container base image uses an OS distribution whose OpenSSL provider has a FIPS 140-3 validation, and Echelon records which certificate covers the deployed version and whether the module runs in its validated (FIPS) mode. Echelon states precisely which operations use validated modules and does not claim 'FIPS compliant' for the whole service. Where a customer contractually requires FIPS mode end to end, it is offered for a dedicated cell after testing that all dependencies operate correctly in that mode.
intended_practice: Choose base image and provider services with validated modules; maintain a certificate register.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: key management in FIPS 140-3 validated HSMs and use of validated platform cryptographic modules, with an exact list of covered operations. Not yet implemented; Echelon makes no FIPS validation claim today.
residual_risks: Validated module versions lag OS updates; patching OpenSSL can move the deployed version outside the validated certificate, creating a conflict between patching and validation.
open_questions: Does any target customer contractually require FIPS 140-3 validated modules (for example public-sector or federal-adjacent work)?
Which base image distribution and OpenSSL provider will be used, and what is its CMVP certificate status?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want assurance that cryptography is correctly implemented and uses approved algorithms.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Weak or flawed cryptographic implementation exposing data.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: FIPS validation proves a module was tested at a version and configuration; it does not prove correct use by the application, and validated versions often lag security patches.
challenge.legally_required: Required for US federal systems and contractors handling federal data; not required by statute for DAF sponsors, wealth managers or most banks' vendors. Some state and higher-education buyers adopt it.
challenge.contractually_required: Some bank and public-sector contracts require FIPS 140 validated encryption; many questionnaires ask about it.
challenge.historical_convention: FIPS 140 has been the US government benchmark since the 1990s and is used as a proxy for crypto quality.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Using only platform crypto through restricted .NET APIs (ANS-ENC-009) removes custom implementations by construction; algorithm choices are fixed in code.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Analyzers and a CBOM verify only approved algorithms are used.
challenge.continuous_evidence: The CBOM per release shows algorithms, modules and versions in use.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Approved-algorithm enforcement plus validated HSMs for key custody; validated mode in the application only where contractually required.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If a customer is under federal requirements, validation is mandatory and the alternative is irrelevant.
challenge.conventional_cost: Running FIPS mode everywhere: medium, plus compatibility testing and delayed patching.
challenge.alternative_risks: Answer precision may be read as evasion by checklist reviewers.
supporting_arguments: Correct use and current patches matter more than module certificates for actual risk.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely for most private customers if the answer is precise; unlikely for customers whose policy literally requires 'FIPS validated' for every module.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Validation is an objective, third-party test that Echelon's own analyzers are not.
Some customers cannot accept anything less, regardless of reasoning.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Customer-managed keys and per-tenant key isolation
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-006 and UNB-TEN-008 require partner-scoped encryption keys and per-partner key management where contracted; not implemented.
target_answer: Every sponsor tenant has its own key-encryption key, so keys and therefore cryptographic access are isolated per tenant even in shared databases. For sponsors who contract for it, the tenant key can be a customer-managed key in the sponsor's own cloud KMS account, granted to Unbound for encrypt and decrypt only; the sponsor can audit every use and revoke the grant, which renders its data unreadable to Unbound (with documented consequences for service, legal holds and records retention). Echelon does not offer hold-your-own-key arrangements where keys are outside any cloud KMS, because Unbound's authoritative ledger must remain available for payments and regulatory records.
intended_practice: Design per-tenant key hierarchy in ADR-006; offer customer-managed keys only after operational procedures and revocation consequences are tested.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: a separate encryption key per sponsor, with optional sponsor-controlled keys by contract. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: A sponsor revoking its key during an incident or dispute would stop payments and statement delivery for its funds; contract terms must address this.
Customer-managed keys in another cloud account create a cross-account dependency and a new outage mode.
open_questions: Will any sponsor require customer-managed keys at launch, and is cross-provider (sponsor uses a different cloud) support needed?

challenge.customer_intent: Large sponsors want control over their data's confidentiality, including the ability to cut off the vendor.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Vendor insider, vendor compromise, or legal compulsion exposes sponsor data; or vendor relationship ends badly.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Customer-managed keys give a revocation lever and audit visibility, but the vendor's application still sees plaintext while operating, so they do not protect against a compromised vendor application.
challenge.legally_required: Not required by US law for DAF sponsors or banks' vendors.
challenge.contractually_required: Occasionally requested by large financial institutions.
challenge.historical_convention: BYOK became a premium SaaS feature as cloud adoption raised sovereignty concerns.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Per-tenant keys (without customer custody) already give cryptographic tenant isolation and enable per-tenant crypto-shredding at exit.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Key policies are enforced by KMS, not by application code.
challenge.continuous_evidence: KMS logs show every use of each tenant key.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Per-tenant keys for all, customer-managed keys only where contracted.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, through key inventory and KMS logs.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If a customer's threat model includes the running vendor application, neither option suffices.
challenge.conventional_cost: Customer-managed keys: high engineering and support cost.
challenge.alternative_cost: Per-tenant keys: medium, mostly within ADR-006 work.
challenge.alternative_risks: Customer revocation can make records unavailable that the sponsor is legally required to retain.
supporting_arguments: Per-tenant keys deliver most of the isolation benefit at lower operational risk.

Revocation is the only control that survives a contract dispute.

title: Secrets management and prevention of hardcoded secrets
status_rationale: SEC-CRYPTO-001 prohibits hardcoded secrets and calls for secret scanning and rotation; SOC2-003 prohibits secrets in logs; no secret store or scanning pipeline exists for Unbound.
target_answer: Unbound holds no long-lived secrets where platform identity can replace them: workloads authenticate to the database, KMS and cloud services with platform-issued short-lived credentials. Remaining secrets (third-party API keys, webhook signing secrets, provider credentials) live in a managed secret store, are retrieved at runtime by the workload identity that needs them, are never written to source, configuration files, container images, IaC state, logs or AI agent context, and rotate on a defined schedule and on personnel change or suspected exposure. Secret scanning runs on every commit and on history, blocking merges; a found secret is treated as compromised and rotated, not just removed. Logging redacts secret-typed values by construction because secrets are wrapped in a type whose string rendering is masked.
current_practice: Not established for Unbound. Whether secret scanning runs on Echelon repositories is not verified.
intended_practice: Adopt secret store with hosting decision; enable secret scanning in Praxis CI workflow now for existing repositories.
customer_statement: Planned: no hardcoded secrets, a managed secret store, automatic rotation, and blocking secret scanning on every commit. Not yet established.
residual_risks: Secret scanners miss custom-format secrets; scanning is detective, so the typed-secret and platform-identity design carries more weight.
open_questions: Is secret scanning enabled on Echelon's existing repositories today?

title: Field-level encryption of donor PII and bank account numbers
status_rationale: UNB-DATA-007 proposes a segregated encrypted identity vault; UNB-PAY-005 requires secrets and privacy protection for bank details; nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Restricted fields, including bank account and routing numbers, tax identifiers, dates of birth and government ID data, are encrypted at the application layer before reaching PostgreSQL, using AES-256-GCM with per-tenant data keys from KMS (ANS-ENC-004) and the record identifier bound as associated data so ciphertext cannot be moved between records. In F#, these fields are distinct types (for example an EncryptedBankAccountNumber) with private constructors, so a plaintext value cannot be stored, logged or serialized by mistake; plaintext exists only inside the narrow payment-preparation and verification paths that need it. Display uses masked values (last four digits). Equality search uses a keyed HMAC index, never the plaintext. Donor PII sits in a segregated identity store so the append-only event history refers to it by token rather than embedding it (UNB-DATA-007), which enables lawful erasure by key destruction (ANS-ENC-011). This also satisfies the Nacha requirement that account numbers used for ACH be rendered unreadable when stored electronically, to the extent that requirement applies to Unbound as a third-party service provider.
intended_practice: Build the typed encrypted-field module and identity vault as part of ADR-006 before any real bank data is accepted.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: bank account numbers and other restricted donor data encrypted at the field level with per-sponsor keys, masked in display, and excluded from logs by design. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: The application process can decrypt; a compromise of the running application or its identity exposes plaintext for the tenants it serves.
Keyed HMAC indexes on low-entropy values (for example short account numbers) can be brute-forced if the HMAC key leaks.
open_questions: Is Unbound's ACH volume as a third-party service provider expected to reach the Nacha account-number-protection thresholds, and does the sponsor's ODFI agreement impose the requirement regardless of volume?
Which fields are classified restricted (data classification is owned by DCL)?

title: Approved cryptography only: no custom cryptography and restricted .NET cryptographic APIs
status_rationale: SEC-CRYPTO-001 prohibits custom cryptographic algorithms; SEC-LANG-001 makes F# the default language; neither has implemented enforcement.
target_answer: Echelon code uses no custom cryptographic algorithms, protocols or constructions (SEC-CRYPTO-001). All cryptographic operations go through one small, reviewed F# module that exposes only purpose-level functions (encrypt field, sign evidence, hash for integrity, derive password verifier) built on .NET's System.Security.Cryptography types backed by the platform library: AES-GCM for authenticated encryption, SHA-256/384/512 for hashing, HMAC-SHA-256, ECDSA P-256/P-384 or RSA-PSS for signatures, RandomNumberGenerator for all randomness, and PBKDF2 with high iteration counts only where a password-based key is unavoidable (user passwords are handled by the identity provider). Direct use of System.Security.Cryptography elsewhere, of obsolete types (MD5, SHA-1 for security purposes, DES, TripleDES, RC2, ECB or CBC without authentication, System.Random for security values) and of certificate-validation overrides is blocked by an analyzer gate. Because Roslyn analyzers do not analyze F# code, the gate requires an F# analyzer (FSharp.Analyzers.SDK) or a compiled-assembly check; this is a known tooling gap. Cryptographic code changes require review by a second engineer with cryptography competence.
current_practice: Not established. The rule exists only as proposed policy text.
intended_practice: Write the crypto module and banned-API check before any cryptographic feature is built.
customer_statement: Echelon's proposed standard prohibits custom cryptography and requires approved libraries. Enforcement tooling is planned and not yet built.
residual_risks: Analyzers can be bypassed through reflection or native interop; SEC-LANG-001 and SEC-EXEC-001 restrict those separately.
Correct primitives can still be misused (nonce reuse in AES-GCM); the purpose-level API and property tests address this.
open_questions: Which F# analyzer or IL-level tool will enforce the banned-API list, and has its detection been benchmarked (scanner validation per the Standard)?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want cryptography to be standard, current and correctly used.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Homegrown or misused cryptography leading to decryptable data or forgeable signatures.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: A written cryptography policy listing approved algorithms is common but rarely enforced in code; reviewers cannot see whether developers follow it.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires a crypto policy document; PCI DSS Req 12.3.3 requires a cryptographic cipher suite and protocol inventory where card data is in scope.
challenge.contractually_required: Questionnaires ask for a cryptographic standard or policy.
challenge.historical_convention: Policy documents were the only practical control when cryptography was scattered across codebases.
challenge.architectural_elimination: A single purpose-level module with banned APIs elsewhere removes direct primitive use from application code within scope.

challenge.continuous_evidence: Each release produces analyzer results and a cryptographic bill of materials.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Restricted API plus generated inventory, with a short policy that points to them.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, once the analyzer exists and is validated.

challenge.invalidating_conditions: If the F# analyzer gap is not closed, enforcement is weaker than claimed.

challenge.alternative_cost: Analyzer and module development: low to medium.
challenge.alternative_risks: Concentrating crypto in one module raises the impact of a bug in that module.

opposing_arguments: F# analyzer ecosystem is immature compared with C#; claimed enforcement may have gaps.
Auditors still expect a policy document.

title: Cryptographic agility and post-quantum readiness
status_rationale: No cryptographic inventory exists. Unbound retains donor and financial records for long periods, which makes harvest-now-decrypt-later relevant for data in transit.
target_answer: Echelon maintains a cryptographic bill of materials generated from code and configuration for every release: algorithms, key sizes, protocols, libraries and where each is used. Because primitives are reached only through the purpose-level crypto module (ANS-ENC-009) and keys are versioned in KMS, an algorithm can be replaced by changing the module and re-wrapping or re-encrypting data under a new key version without touching business logic. Ciphertexts and signatures carry algorithm and key version identifiers. Echelon tracks NIST's post-quantum standards and the deprecation timeline for quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms, enables hybrid post-quantum key exchange in TLS when the edge provider and .NET platform support it, prioritizing external connections that carry long-lived sensitive data, and plans migration of signing keys (evidence, statements, builds) to post-quantum signature schemes as KMS support becomes available. Symmetric encryption at AES-256 is considered adequate against known quantum attacks.
intended_practice: Generate a CBOM from the first build; record a PQC migration plan.
customer_statement: Planned: a generated cryptographic inventory and an algorithm-agile design so that post-quantum algorithms can be adopted as platforms support them. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Post-quantum migration depends on cloud provider, edge provider and .NET platform support timelines outside Echelon's control.
open_questions: Which post-quantum standards and deprecation dates should Echelon cite? NIST FIPS 203/204/205 and NIST IR 8547 are not seeded sources; verify current status before customer use.
When will the selected KMS and edge provider support post-quantum signatures and hybrid key exchange?

title: Cryptographic erasure and key destruction
status_rationale: UNB-DATA-007 proposes cryptographic erasure where lawful; UNB-IMM-008 forbids claiming it works if plaintext exists in backups, logs or exports. Nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Where personal data must be erased but the authoritative event history is append-only, the data is held encrypted under a per-subject or per-tenant key in the identity vault, and erasure is performed by destroying that key in KMS after legal retention and holds are checked. Echelon only claims an erasure is complete when it has verified that no plaintext copy exists in backups, logs, exports, search indexes, AI embeddings or caches within their retention windows, consistent with UNB-IMM-008; otherwise it states the date by which remaining copies expire. Key destruction is two-person approved, logged and evidenced. At sponsor exit, the sponsor's tenant keys are destroyed after the exit package is delivered and retention obligations are confirmed, rendering residual ciphertext unreadable.
intended_practice: Design the identity vault and key-per-subject granularity in ADR-006; involve counsel on retention conflicts (UNB-DATA-007).
customer_statement: Planned: erasure by destruction of the encryption keys protecting personal data, claimed only when no plaintext copies remain. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Per-subject keys at scale increase KMS cost and complexity; data-key wrapping under a tenant key reduces cost but changes erasure granularity.
Provider KMS key deletion waiting periods delay final destruction.
open_questions: Will counsel accept cryptographic erasure as deletion for state privacy law and contractual purposes?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want assurance that deleted data is truly gone, including at contract end.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Residual data remains accessible after deletion or exit.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Physical media sanitization and overwrite procedures do not apply to cloud storage Echelon does not control; vendor deletion certificates are attestations, not proof.
challenge.legally_required: State privacy laws grant deletion rights in some cases; retention laws for charitable and financial records may conflict (UNB-DATA-007 requires counsel review).
challenge.contractually_required: Contracts commonly require return and deletion of data at termination with a certificate.
challenge.historical_convention: Deletion certificates and media destruction were designed for owned hardware.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Destroying keys makes all ciphertext copies unreadable at once, including copies in backups that cannot be selectively edited.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: KMS enforces destruction and logs it.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Key destruction events are verifiable records.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Cryptographic erasure with verified plaintext-copy inventory, recognized in NIST SP 800-88 as a sanitization technique.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, if the plaintext-copy inventory is complete.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If any plaintext copy exists outside the encrypted vault, the claim is false (UNB-IMM-008).
challenge.conventional_cost: Manual deletion across stores and backups: high and unverifiable.
challenge.alternative_risks: Accidental key destruction is irreversible data loss; two-person approval and waiting periods are essential.
supporting_arguments: Works for immutable stores and backups where record-level deletion is impossible.

opposing_arguments: Hard to prove no plaintext leaked into logs or embeddings.
Some reviewers do not recognize cryptographic erasure as deletion.

title: Signing keys for builds, evidence, statements and ledger integrity anchors
status_rationale: CNV-PLT-010 requires signed builds and daily external anchoring of ledger digests; REQ-X-033 proposes cryptographic verification of statements; UNB-XIN-SAS-004 assigns signing key ids to webhook subscriptions. Nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Separate signing keys, each held non-exportably in KMS/HSM, sign: release artifacts and provenance (CNV-PLT-010); control evidence bundles; issued statement manifests (REQ-X-033); outbound webhook deliveries (UNB-XIN-SAS-004); and daily ledger digest anchors published externally (CNV-PLT-010). Each key has one purpose, a named owner, rotation schedule and published public key with validity periods so customers and auditors can verify signatures independently. Verification is automated: deployments reject unsigned artifacts, and an anchor checker compares ledger digests to published anchors daily.
intended_practice: Define signing key inventory and verification flows with the evidence architecture.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: purpose-specific signing keys in hardware-backed key management for builds, evidence, statements and ledger integrity, with public verification. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Compromise of the build signing key would let an attacker produce artifacts that pass deployment verification.
open_questions: Where will ledger digest anchors be published so that they are independent of Echelon's own infrastructure?
